Madam Speaker, for years the Progressive Conservative Party has been urging that the icebreaker fleet of the Canadian Coast Guard be upgraded. Not only will the procurement of new icebreaking vessels enable the Coast Guard to fulfil its obligations in the St. Lawrence and Arctic more adequately, resulting in safer and longer shipping seasons and generally stimulating commercial navigation, but also it will provide badly needed work for hard-pressed Canadian shipyard workers. For these reasons we on this side are pleased to see the Government finally
acting on our recommendations and placing orders for six light icebreaking vessels.
The next step, might I suggest, Madam Speaker, should be the design and construction of heavy icebreakers for year-round use in the Arctic Ocean and Northwest Passage.

The U.S. Ambassador to Canada, Paul Robinson, Jr., has recently stated that things are going very well between this Government and the Reagan administration. The American trade representative, William Block, has been quoted as saying that Canada-U.S. relations are strong and thriving. Mr. Block said that issues between the two countries are being addressed in a spirit of co-operation.

The United States has applauded the new trade policy of this Government, which calls for an increase in free trade between the two countries. That trade policy recognizes the United States as Canada's best trading partner and strongest ally.

There are other signs of a healthy relationship. Canada and the United States are working together in a serious and co-operative spirit to combat the problem of acid rain. Madam Speaker, I continue to voice my concern about youth unemployment. As recently as 1981 youth unemployment was running at a rate of 13.3 per cent. Last year it moved up to 18.7 per cent. According to the OECD it will average 22 per cent this year and next. This pretty well reflects the statistics in my own riding of Parry Sound-Muskoka. The over-all message from the OECD is that the magnitude of the unemployment problem left over from the recession is overwhelming.
This problem is particularly serious for young people who shoulder the major part of the burden of a global recession and high unemployment. As the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has already observed, frustration and apathy among the young could lead to social discontent. With respect to my own riding of Parry Sound-Muskoka, great concern is not enough.

Madam Speaker, I MO, like its sister organization, the International Civil Aviation Organization, ICAO, which has its headquarters in Montreal, is concerned with the promotion of safety. With ICAO it is air safety, with I MO it is safety of life at sea.
As one of the world's largest trading nations, Canada draws upon maritime services to transport over 200 million tons of international commerce annually. Domestic waterborne trading exceeds 65 million tons annually. With over 500 active ports and harbours, Canada annually hosts approximately 60,000 commercial vessel arrivals. The safe and effective administration of this country's maritime environment is entrusted to our Canadian Coast Guard whose members are globally recognized for their professionalism. subsubtopic: WHITE FARM EQUIPMENT LTD.-DEALERS" OFFER TO BUY COMPANY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, a Manitoba businessman named John Buhler, and other White Farm Equipment dealers, are making a serious attempt to retain White Farm Limited as a viable separate entity. Last night Mr. Buhler telexed a letter of intent to buy, along with a deposit of $100,000, to the receiver. He plans to assemble a $11.6 million offer in conjunction with other White Farm
September 30, 1983

dealers and possibly a financier. But, Madam Speaker, he needs more time.
I urge the federal Government either to view this letter of intent as a legal, solid offer, or to extend the deadline from 9 a.m. tomorrow, Saturday, until October 15, by which time Mr. Buhler expects to have ironed out the details. At stake is the fate of 119 White Farm dealerships. There are also the thousands of farmers who own White Farm equipment and require replacement parts for that equipment, who must be considered.
This latest offer is especially important to my home Province of Manitoba, where there are 20 White Farm dealerships employing more than 200 people. Relocating the company s assets in Manitoba, as Mr. Buhler has proposed, would place the headquarters in the very region where the products are in high demand.
The Government has already seen to it that an offer to purchase by White Farm's parent company in the United States was rejected. 1 urge the Government therefore not to let this offer also slip through its hands.

Madam Speaker, tomorrow women and men across the country will mark a day of action for "Choice on Abortion". The issue is choice, not pro or anti-abortion. The right of the indvidual male or female to exercise freedom of choice in private medical and sexual matters is a hallmark of Canadian society. The Badgley Report documented economic and geographic inequities in the abortion law. Fewer than 30 per cent of hospitals in Canada perform abortions. Increasing numbers of women must obtain abortions in the U.S. Prevention of unwanted pregnancies, of course, is preferable to abortion. If birth control information, education and counselling were more readily available, the number of abortions would decrease. However, the federal Government has been steadily eroding Planned Parenthood's funding.
In 1982, 72 per cent of Canadians believed that the decision to perform an abortion should rest with the consenting patient and her doctor. Ninety-five per cent of doctors approve of abortion in some circumstances. The Canadian Labour Congress, the United Church, and the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women support the removal of abortion from the Criminal Code.

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance and it is further to the concerns expressed yesterday about the very high level of the budget deficit. I recently read a compilation of 16 leading North American economists who all expressed the same concern about the very high level of deficits and the effect this has on the economy. Their conclusion was that we would either have record high interest rates, a crowding out of private sector borrowers and high inflation, or an aborted recovery. Since that is the conclusion he will have to deal with whether he likes it or not, what action is he proposing to take to deal with this, since his budget of last April clearly has not been enough?
[DOT] (U25)

Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member is quite right in making reference to the fact that most analysts in the United States in particular, and in Canada as well, feel that the size of the deficit is important in terms of the performance of the economy over the medium and long term. I have indicated this in my own budget and I have taken a number of steps in that regard. In the speech I made to the International Monetary Fund 1 also indicated that this was a very important issue to be addressed in North America over the next while.
If my hon. friend would check the statements of the analysts he has referred to, he will find that practically all of them have mentioned this as a medium-term problem and not as a
Oral Questions
short-term problem, and that there is no crowding out of private investors at the present time and none is expected this year. Most analysts do not expect that there will be a serious problem in this regard at least until late next year.
In my own budget I have taken steps to reduce the deficit gradually over the next few years. As the Hon. Member knows, the plans contained in my budget have been very well received by the country and by the financial markets as being a responsible step to gradually moderating the size of the deficit.

Madam Speaker, I think the Minister is living in the past again, it is clear that the commentary we have been hearing has suggested that this recovery, which is very tentative right now, will be aborted.

Madam Speaker, let me refer back to the conclusions reached by the Conference Board a couple of days ago. Those conclusions indicated that the unemployment rate in Canada relative to that in the United States would decline far more slowly and would still be around 11 per cent in five years' time. That is clearly related to the level of interest rates over that period of time. Is the Minister doing anything to address this problem, or will he consign to a further five years of misery those one and a half million Canadians who are out of work today?

Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member chooses to refer to one report made by one organization. He neglects to refer to reports made by the 18 other organizations that have taken somewhat different views in this regard. I can refer him to a statement made by the former head of the C.D. Howe Institute, Judith Maxwell, who has taken a very different view.
Rather than engaging in a battle of forecasters with my hon. friend, I would invite him to look at the facts. He will see, for instance, that our interest rates, in spite of the large deficit that exists this year, have declined since the beginning of the year. I hope that they will continue to decline gradually. What is even more important is that our interest rates have declined significantly compared to those in the United States.
The spread that formerly existed between U.S. and Canada interest rates has narrowed extensively for short-term papers. We now have an interest rate in this country which is half a point below that in the United States. I think the Canadian economy has performed very well in that regard. The world financial institutions and the Canadian people at large are showing a great deal more confidence in the country than my hon. friend seems to be showing.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have already indicated to my Hon. colleague that 1 am always glad to meet those who are responsible for our financial institutions in Canada, including banks or any other organization, if that can be helpful in improving the economic situation in Canada. I would also remind the Hon. Member that, as I said earlier, we have brought down interest rates in Canada very rapidly during the past year, and that at the present time, the prime rate in Canada is the same as in the United States, despite the fact that our inflation rate here in Canada is higher than it is in the States, even today. I have always tried to keep interest rates as low as possible in this country, and that has been the objective of the monetary and fiscal policy we have pursued since last year, and we intend to continue our efforts to reduce interest rates as much as possible. speechtext:
Petro-Canada International Assistance Corporation reports as follows:
1.	Petro-Canada International was initially incorporated under the Canada Business Corporations Act on January 20, 1981, pursuant to the Petro-Canada Act. PCI's mandate, which is to act as a delivery mechanism for Canadian official development assistance to oil-importing developing countries, was established by Order in Council P.C. 1981-2167, dated August 5, 1981. The Articles of Incorporation were subsequently amended on November 18, 1981 to reflect the directives of the Government and on April 22, 1982, through Order in Council P.C. 1982-1264, the Corporation's name was changed to Petro-Canada International Assistance Corporation.
2.	Terms of reference: (a) Assist developing countries to reduce or eliminate their dependence on imported oil by using Canadian technology and expertise, where possible, for hydrocarbon exploration and related activities, and function as a direct-delivery mechanism for Canadian official development assistance and, as an executing agent for other development assistance institutions, to carry out the following activities in developing countries eligible to receive Canadian bilateral development assistance and which are dependent on imported oil:
(i)	to participate in exploration for hydrocarbon resources, particularly oil and gas, in developing countries;
(ii)	to conduct pre-exploration and related studies in developing countries; and
(iii)	to provide technical assistance and training to personnel from developing countries in hydrocarbon resource exploration development and production-related activities.
(b)	Operate as an instrument of Canadian official development assistance in a manner consistent with the government's foreign aid objectives and programs.
3.	(a) PCIAC is financed by funds appropriated by Parliament under the spending estimates of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources.
(b)	PCAC's one share is held by its parent, Petro-Canada.
(c)	Under the Articles of Incorporation, prior to the commencement of PCIAC's financial year, the Corporation must submit a capital budget for the approval of the Governor in Council, on the recommendation of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, the Minister of Finance, and the President of the Treasury Board and an operating budget to the Government for the approval of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and the President of the Treasury Board. However, at the present time, PCIAC provides assistance in the form of grants only and does not submit a capital budget. The 1982 operating budget for PCIAC was $21 million, and the 1983 budget has been set at $42 million.
(d)	The Articles of Incorporation stipulate that PCIAC cannot borrow money without the approval of the Governor in Council, on the recommendation of the Minister of Energy,
Order Paper Questions
Mines and Resources and the President of the Treasury Board. There is, however, a provision for an advance or loan from Petro-Canada which in the aggregate cannot exceed $50 million.
4.	(a) and (b) The Board of Directors of PCIAC is William J. Jenkins, Wilbert H. Hopper, Frederick G. Rayer, Peter M. Towe, George W. Tough. The Directors do not receive any remuneration.
The Officers of PCIAC are Frederick G. Rayer, President, Georges A. Leger, Vice-President, Peter M. Towe, Chairman, Robert McCaskill, Secretary. These officers are employees of Petro-Canada, which charges PCIAC monthly for their services on a non-profit, cost-recovery basis according to the time actually spent on the business of the Corporation.
(c)	To date, meetings of the Board of Directors have been held in Ottawa.
5.	PCIAC was instructed to utilize Canadian technology and expertise where possible in the development and implementation of projects that would assist developing countries to reduce or eliminate their dependency on imported oil. A major criterion for consideration of any project by PCIAC's Board of Directors is the potential for the use of Canadian goods and services.
6.	(a) and (b) Prospective recipient countries submit project proposals for consideration through official channels. In reviewing these project proposals, the following criteria are used: the eligibility of the country for Canadian aid; the potential for the use of Canadian goods and services; the geological potential; the energy needs of the recipient country; the domestic economics of the proposed project; the potential social and economic benefits of a reduced dependency on imported oil; and the level of private sector activity in the recipient country.

7.	PCIAC reports to Petro-Canada.

DEBATES________________________________________27621
Western Grain Transportation Act

The House resumed from Thursday, September 29, consideration of Bill C-155, an Act to facilitate the transportation, shipping and handling of western grain and to amend certain Acts in consequence thereof, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Transport; and Motions Nos. 24, 25 and 29 (Mr. Benjamin).

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: 1 understand the Hon. Member for Dauphin-Swan River (Mr. Lewycky) had the floor when this matter was last debated and 1 believe he has approximately four minutes remaining.

Mr. Speaker, that is correct. When we reached six o'clock last night 1 was just trying to point out to the House that if the wording in the amendment as printed in Bill C-155 remains, this would constitute an attack on the co-operative spirit of the farmers of western Canada. 1 want to just underline the problem with the present wording as we have it in the amended and reprinted Bill.
The particular problem I want to highlight is that any of the farmers who are members of a local shipping committee or who are Wheat Pool delegates, those who might be officers of perhaps even a co-operative farm, farmers who are co-operating with other farmers, would be effectively excluded from eligibility for being elected as members of the Senior Grain Transportation Committee. Our suggested solution, Mr. Speaker, is that we strike out the reference to co-operatives, which would strike them off the excluded list, thus making them eligible to participate on the Senior Grain Transportation Committee.
By way of background, Mr. Speaker, if we were to let the present wording remain in the amended Bill we are really betraying a cultural bias, albeit an eastern cultural bias, and I suppose this would be a good time to introduce to Hon. Members the concept of ethnocentrism. That is something we teach at any elementary sociology course at the university level. Basically it means we judge other cultures, or even regional subcultures, on the basis of our own experience. I suggest that if we were to leave this wording in here, that is really what is happening in this particular case. There would be a failure on the part of this Parliament as drafters of this legislation to recognize and understand unique Prairie institutions which have developed over the years co-operatively and in a pioneer spirit. Therefore we are suggesting that it is all the more important that we strike out co-operatives from this list of individuals who are excluded.
I am a bit embarrassed to say that it was the original amendment of the Hon. Member for Kindersley-Lloydminster (Mr. McKnight) which excluded people who are members of co-ops and local shipping committees. What 1 am suggesting is
27622	______________________________ COMMONS DEBATES
Western Grain Transportation Act
that our amendment gives a second chance to the Government and to the Conservatives to right a fault which may have been unintentional; I give them the benefit of the doubt. However, in any case it is giving them and the Government an opportunity to correct a fault that really should not have been there in the first place.
I would like to elaborate a little further on the other motion that has been grouped with Motion No. 24, and that is Motion No. 29. If one were to ask me what our amendment would do, its basic intention is to reduce the heavy hand of the CNR and the CPR and to lower their representation on this particular Committee. We do not really think it is necessary that the CPR have a member and the CNR have a member. I think that historically their concerns have been adequately met. There would be an opportunity for producers to ensure that they are not overlooked in the drafting of the Bill.
If Your Honour wants to know why I have expressed concern, it is because we have been through a series of rail line abandonment hearings, for example, in Manitoba. 1 know that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Axworthy) is aware that there have been some 18 hearings dealing with rail line abandonment in Manitoba and all 18 have been in favour of the railways. The railways are adequately represented in the CTC, which has looked after the interest of the railways. Why is it that the last 18 hearings all went in favour of the railways?
1 see Your Honour is giving me the signal that my allotted time is about to expire. 1 am simply saying that if our amendments are accepted, there would be an opportunity for both the Government and the Conservative Party to right a historic wrong and ensure that the producers would be adequately represented. 1 just give those few suggestions to the House of Commons so that we could correct some of these obvious faults in the amended, reprinted wording of the Bill.

If Your Honour will notice, our Motion No. 25, while it covers the same areas as our Motions Nos. 26 and 27, calls for five members, not six. This is the problem with the groupings. would like to ask if Your Honour could just leave this matter in abeyance until Monday and we could discuss it further.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The Chair would accept the Hon. Member's request. I do not hear a procedural argument which would affect the statement I made to the effect that, with the passage of Motion No. 26, it would automatically follow that Motion No. 25 would be withdrawn. However, if the Hon. Member wants further time to consider the problem, then there is no difficulty. It will not interfere in any way with proceeding with debate on the other motions. Motions Nos. 24 and 29 are for debate now.

Mr. Speaker. I rise in support of Motions Nos. 24 and 29, since I understand we will be pleading Motion No. 25 at a later time.
Briefly, I think the issue at stake here is chiefly whether those who pay are to have an adequate voice in what is done with the money they pay. The question under Motion No. 24 is whether the farmers who have taken the trouble to organize themselves into co-operatives will be penalized and restricted in being able to have representation on the Grain Board. It is apparently the preference of certain Hon. Members to the extreme right that co-operative members and officers should be so penalized, should be kept out of the action, if possible. This would, of course, reduce to some extent the actual grass roots representation of the producers as compared to the carriers. That is the reason for supporting Motion No. 29, which would reduce the railways to one representative.
The fact is that throughout the history of Canada the railroads have been overrepresented in decisions that concern the railroads and the users have been unrepresented. There was some shared of excuse for that when the users were scarcely there in the western Prairies a century ago. There is no excuse for it now.
To reduce the representation those users have had for many years through the co-operatives they have built would be extremely unjust and, in the long run, would turn out to be a mistake economically, because without any doubt the effect of that reduction would be to bias further the policy decisions in favour of the carriers, especially the Canadian Pacific Railway, and against the producing farmers. The bias has already gone farther than is healthy, but this kind of unfair redistribution of the powers of the board would increase it further so that decisions would be more unfair and more uneconomical.
If the farmers are unable to represent themselves adequately in the struggle over both freight rates and the application of the moneys that are spent on capital and operating of the railroad so far as grain is concerned, if their voices are muffled by the present proposal, then the farmers and the grain industry will suffer. The industry will decline as a result of the kind of action which our amendments seek to prevent.
What is at stake here is also a deeper principle which runs far beyond the Prairies. It is the principle of user-pay. We have heard this slogan, especially from certain government spokesmen over the last ten years, that the users should pay. It is usually focused on some particular area. At this point it is
September 30, 1983

being focused on the prairie farmers who constitute a minority within Canada. There is a big propaganda campaign to accuse the prairie farmers of being fat cats who want someone else to pay for transporting their grain so that they can receive unearned income by not paying a fair share of the cost of transportation. It has not been mentioned, however, that practically every other form of transportation in Canada is also subsidized. Airline, marine and road transportation particularly is lavishly subsidized. If user-pay were to be applied against everyone who uses our highways, rides our airlines or uses the St. Lawrence Seaway or the rest of our marine transportation, there would be a unanimous outcry against that policy. It would be quite uneconomical for the majority of users, whether they are passengers or freight consignors and consignees. Therefore the policy of applying the principle of user-pay is handled selectively.
Approximately five years ago this policy was implemented in metro Toronto as a justification for jacking up the fares on the transit system and establishing an almost annual fixed increase in the TTC fares. The slogan at that time was "user-pay". It was pointed out in that case that if no one used the TTC, the roads would be congested to the point where the automobile drivers would be unable to use the roads. Therefore it was in the interest of not only TTC riders but the public that TTC be able to operate with a fare that even poor people could pay.
The same dispute applies in the case of the grain growers and the grain carriers. We see here an attempt on the part of the Government, and certain movers of Conservative amendments in league with the Government, to stick it to those farmers who have had the courage and sense of social responsibility to organize the co-operatives. These co-operatives which handle approximately 60 per cent of the grain will be penalized. They are to be denied effective representation on this board and clearly, the import of that type of change is to hand over the decision-making more powerfully than ever to the Canadian Pacific Railroad, Canadian Pacific Investments and those associated with milking the farmers.
It is the farmers who are to be milked by this Bill. If this Bill passes, there will no doubt be other targets picked up very quickly. We know that the effect of the Government's policy which was stated two years ago is to undo all the aid arrangements on which Canada's transportation networks have been built. The argument in the back rooms is probably to the effect that, since farmers are now established in the Prairies and Canadian cities are filled with people, there is a captive market for the profiteering owners of the transportation industries. These industries include those who either profit from direct transportation or supply the expensive equipment for publicly-owned corporations such as the Toronto Transit Commission. In either case the aim is to use a captive market, whether it be the farmers in Saskatchewan or the transit riders in metro Toronto, who must use the established transportation system because there is no alternative. These systems have become a monopoly which they must use.
Western Grain Transportation Act
Since there is an established market with no chance of competition, the corporation owners, their friends across the aisle and to my extreme right have decided that now is the time to begin sticking it to the users and raising the price they will have to pay regardless of the fact that on the Prairies, for example, farmers' income has declined by over 40 per cent in the last six years while the income of Canadian Pacific has risen by some 250 per cent. Those facts are being studiously ignored in the propaganda we hear from the large Parties in this House and their friends in the media.
However, if they have their way, it will be a short ride even for those corporations because once they have starved the farmers out of business there will not be any grain to haul. They will not be able to play with the Crow rate any longer. It is a short-sighted policy even from their point of view but it is disastrous not only for the farmers but for the Canadian people. I urge Parliament to think very carefully about these amendments and particularly to support Motions Nos. 24 and 29.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to have an opportunity to say a few words this afternoon in this very important debate. I am particularly pleased to speak to this particular amendment that has been put forward by my colleague for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin).
1 believe that the issue we are dealing with today touches the very basis of how we see a democratic society. I do not believe there are any Members in the House, and 1 would like to think that there are not many Canadians, who do not strongly and firmly believe in the principles of a democracy. One of those basic principles is that Canadians ought to have a voice in what is decided by those groups that have an opportunity to make a profound impact on their lives. That is essentially what we are talking about here today-whether 15,000 to 20,000 western Canadians should be denied representation on one of the most crucial boards that deals with western grain transportation.
Quite frankly, I find that perplexing, to say the least. It is dificult to understand why the Government would say that there are perhaps as many as 20,000 people in western Canada who ought not to participate in the democratic process over a matter that will have a profound influence on their lives and futures.
I know that some Members opposite and other Members of the House may question my assumption that 20,000 people will be affected. Let me say that 1 have a legal opinion-I emphasize "legal" opinion-which states that this is the case. It is that person's legal opinion that 15,000 to 20,000 western Canadian grain producers will not be able to take part in the appropriate elections to see them represented on a board that will be most influential on the lives of western Canadians.
I suggest this is a direct attack on the co-operative movement in western Canada. 1 do not want to suggest for a moment that the Government is doing this with some malicious intent or evil motivation. I would like to think that it is

September 30, 1983
Western Grain Transportation Act simply an oversight on behalf of the Minister and the federal Government that the co-operatives ought not to have a voice, in terms of grain transportation, equal to that of others who are involved.
Those of us who come from western Canada and have lived on the Prairies of western Canada recognize the importance of the co-operative movement only too well. I would go so far as to say that it was the co-operative movement in western Canada that built a good deal of that part of the country. That co-operative movement has probably meant more to lifting the welfare of Canadians generally than any other movement in this country.
I believe the very essence of co-operatives has been overlooked over the years. I recall very distinctly that the federal Government realized not many months ago that most people from western Canada were involved in co-operatives. The co-operative movement, as part of the western tradition, has become an integral part of westerners' lives.
At the point when the federal Government recognized the integral relationship between the co-operatives and life in western Canada, it decided to make a direct appeal for the support of the co-operative movement. It did a number of things over the last number of months that would appeal to the co-operatives in western Canada and would appeal to co-operatives generally, although it did focus on gathering more support from that sector of western Canadian society. That is why I am perplexed today, Mr. Speaker.
I am somewhat confused about why the Government of Canada would bring forth such a notion in order to eliminate participation in some of the most critical decisions facing western Canadians made by people involved in a senior capacity or quasi-management role in the co-operatives. 1 must say that I will be voting against this amendment for no other reason than that it places 15,000 to 20,000 western Canadians in a second-class citizen status. I am not prepared to send a message to that group of people saying that we are not prepared to allow them the democratic right of expressing themselves by running for office in terms of what we are speaking of here today.
I do hope that the Government will come to its senses and realize that the particular amendment of which I am speaking is intended to assist the Government in providing a more democratic basis for its decision making and that it is not an attempt to scuttle the Government's efforts. In fact, it is an attempt to improve this piece of legislation by recognizing the role of co-operatives and encouraging people to participate on the appropriate board.

Mr. Speaker, 1 am rising to support the amendments put forward in the name of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin), being Motions Nos. 24 and 29. I would argue, as some of my colleagues have argued, that the very idea that representatives of the Wheat Pools should not be nominees is
offensive to any Hon. Member of the House who has fought for some time to ensure that the people who have a great stake in the outcome-the producers or representatives of producers-should have some say in those major decisions that affect the operations of their farms and that affect their livelihoods, and I am certainly one of those Members. That the Government and the Official Opposition can argue that directors, agents or representatives of any co-operative should not be allowed to become a member of the Senior Grain Transportation Committee is mystifying, to say the least.
Members of many of the co-operatives concerned here have a very direct interest in the number of cars allocated to them and where those cars will be allocated. This is not because they have personal vested interests but because they are representatives or directors of co-operatives that broadly represent the interests of that whole group of producers. Those representatives are only to be some of the representatives on that committee, but surely it is not too much to suggest that they, above all, should have some major say, if not the determining say, in the allocation of grain cars. There have been shortages of cars for the Canadian grain industry in the past. I know that many of those cars are also allocated from time to time to the lumber industry in my own area. Surely the railway companies should not have a greater say in the allocation of those cars than the democratically elected representatives of those thousands of people whose livelihoods depend on the decisions made.
The attitude of members of the Official Opposition, particularly as so many of them represent the western grain growing Provinces, is absolutely astounding. As I was listening to yesterday's debate I could not help but recall a play called "Paper Wheat". Unfortunately I do not have the script of that play here today, but in recent years that play enjoyed some popularity and in fact drew crowds right across Canada, particularly in the smaller communities of the prairie Provinces.
The play dealt with the growth of the Wheat Pools and the history of the farmers' movement, particularly in western Canada when farmers attempted to have some determining say as to what would happen to their livelihoods. There was an interesting character in that play. The farmers and others in the farming communities were actively engaged in trying to build the co-ops and the Wheat Pools. They were trying to sign up a certain number of producers in the area in order to establish the Pool. 1 forget the exact target they were aiming for. Perhaps one of my colleagues could help me.
Fifty per cent.

They were trying to sign up 50 per cent of the producers. The interesting character that 1 referred to was a grain elevator operator, and he said when asked to join: "You will never make it". When the farmers signed up 10 per cent of the producers, this fellow said: "No, I am not going to join; you will never make it". They signed up 20 per cent and he said: "No, you will never make it. It's an impossible dream; the railways will beat you and the grain exchange will beat
September 30, 1983

you." The farmers signed up 30 per cent and 40 per cent and this character took the same attitude. Finally the farmers only needed one more member in order to sign up the required 50 per cent of producers. Lo and behold, this fellow decided to join. His comment at that time was: "I always knew they'd do it!"
1 cannot help but think of that particular character in that play, Mr. Speaker, in relation to the position taken by Members of the Official Opposition in relation to this Bill. All of a sudden they have decided, perhaps, that they will vigorously oppose the Bill after having acted in a number of odd ways during the course of the last few months. Do we now hear them saying: "Gee, we always knew they would do it"? Do they want to jump aboard the bandwagon so they do not get left out and they are not seen in the light of their behaviour during the previous few months? They have not really seen the light, have they? They are now taking the position that we should put it off for three years so that they can do it.
Many farmers who are still on the Prairies and have participated in the building of these very co-ops and Wheat Pools will be denied their proper representation unless at least one of these amendments now being moved by members of the NDP or something very much like it is carried. If it is not carried, those farmers will be angry and they will remember. During the long winters on the Canadian Prairies, a lot of thinking gets done. Those farmers will chew over and ruminate on what has been going on during the spring, summer and fall.
One subject that often comes up is "What are those guys in Ottawa doing?" These people have a lot of time to think this over. They are not influenced by the hoopla imagery of the advertising game. They have a memory and they watch the performance of people over the long haul. Like a certain species of the crow, or jackdaw as it is known in some countries, they have a long developed memory. They do not have that instinctively but have gained it through long experience. The working and farming people of prairie Canada will remember who was playing games with their most vital interests.
I ask the Members of the Official Opposition in particular to recognize where they come from and to remember that the farmers of western Canada do not forget easily. I hope the Official Opposition will realize that their prime job is to represent the interests of those who sent them here and will support not only this amendment but a number of others being put forward by the NDP.

Pursuant to Madam Speaker's ruling earlier, Motions Nos. 30, 31, 32, 33, 34 and 35 are to be debated and voted on separately. Motions Nos. 30, 31 and 32 stand in the name of the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin). Accordingly, the debate will begin on Motion No. 30.

Motion No. 30
That Bill C-155 be amended in Clause 3 by adding immediately after line 34 at page 4 the following:
"(/) nothing in paragraph (d) shall prevent elected local committee members and delegates of grain co-operatives and the officers of farming corporations and co-operatives from being eligible for election to the Senior Grain Transportation Committee".
He said: Mr. Speaker, 1 wish to say to those Members who were not participants in the Committee, in case they are not aware of it, that Clause 3 in Part I of the Bill is entirely a clause of the Conservative Party, supported in every paragraph by the Liberals. Not one line, not one word of the Liberal

September 30, 1983
Western Grain Transportation Act
clause was even debated. Members should have seen the original tory Clause 3. It certainly would have eliminated 20,000 to 30,000 grain producers from running for election, those who are of the Wheat Fool committees and UGG locals.
Our legal advice is that the way the clause now reads, it will still prohibit a member of a Wheat Pool committee, the chairman or secretary of a Wheat Pool committee, an elevator agent who holds land and has Wheat Board permit. It will also eliminate a co-operative farm with five or ten farm families on it. It will eliminate members of the board of directors of the co-operative farm, the Chairman of the board and the secretary-treasurer of farm co-operatives from running for election, even though they are otherwise eligible as active grain producers holding a Canadian Wheat Board permit.
My Motion No. 30 will add a new paragraph which reads:
(f) nothing in paragraph (d) shall prevent elected local committee members and delegates of grain co-operatives and the officers of farming corporations and co-operatives from being eligible for election to the Senior Grain Transportation Committee.
I have included farming corporations as well as farming co-operatives because many family farms have incorporated. One spouse may be the president or chairman and the other the secretary or vice-president. Sons and daughters are also part of the incorporation. Our legal advice is that the way the clause now reads, a private farm that is incorporated, whether it be one or more families, grain producers holding a Canadian Wheat Board permit book, would be prohibited from having its members run for election.
As my colleague for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse) pointed out yesterday, there are over 800 Wheat Pool committees in Saskatchewan, each with ten or 20 members. I imagine there are 600 or 700 Wheat Pool committees in Manitoba and in Alberta combined. 1 do not know how many United Grain Growers locals there are. We are looking at between 15,000 and 25,000 grain producers who are eliminated from standing for election to the Senior Grain Transportation Committee the way the clause now reads.
An election under the Bill would now involve four representatives: one from Alberta, two from Saskatchewan and one from Manitoba. The election would be carried out in the same manner as elections for the Canadian Wheat Board Advisory Committee and would probably be carried out at the same time.
In a democratic election, the eligible voters decide who will represent them. It is not up to Parliament. If the president of a grain co-operative who is also a permit book holder and an active grain farmer chooses to run, it will be up to the grain producers in that Province to decide whether they want him. They will decide whether they want somebody who is also on a board of directors, a delegate or a nominee.
This would also eliminate organizations that could hardly be called great friends of mine. They are nice fellows. As the clause now stands, they are prohibited from running. Democratic elections should be kept as wide
as possible. There should be minimum requirements in terms of eligibility. This flies in the face of what 1 consider to be the democratic process.

The way the Committee is now structured under Clause 3, the Senior Grain Transportation Committee will have an inordinate representation of those who do not grow grain and do not hold a Canadian Wheat Board permit.
Each railroad has a representative. There is also one representative each from the Great Lakes carriers, elevator licensees, the Canadian Trucking Association and the Prairie Livestock Feed Board. There is also one for Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba who are also feed grain users. We have only four grain farmers elected at large.
Where were you when we were in Committee?

I am sorry, we have six elevator company representatives now. We are back to the Tory repentance of yesterday. It is incredible to me, Mr. Speaker, that Clause 3, as proposed by the Conservatives and supported by the Government, totally ignores the Government's clause. There they were, joined in an attack on the co-operative movement, and, in other parts of the Bill, in an attack on orderly marketing and the reduction of the authority and powers of the Canadian Wheat Board. That is unacceptable in western Canada, Mr. Speaker.
In their conversion on the road to the Crowsnest Pass the Conservatives have called not for a commutation of the death sentence on the Crow rate but merely a stay of execution. Even that is better than nothing. If it were to succeed it would at least give us three more years of the statutory rate for grain producers. But having done that, it seems to me they have no choice, if they want to have any credibility, particularly in western Canada, but to join us in either forcing the Government to withdraw the legislation or getting the Government to change it so that the statutory grain rates for the producers are kept in place.
The representation of the grain producers on the Senior Grain Transportation Committee has to be kept as wide as possible. That has to be taken care of. There is no reason to impinge upon the eligibility of an active grain producer who currently holds a Canadian Wheat Board permit book; there is no need to impinge upon their ability to run for the position, particularly when the motion moved by the Tories and sup-

No one will convince me, and they will certainly not convince anyone out West, that the Wheat Pools are just a commercial interest and that they do not have the interests of producers at heart. Member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone), trying to tell me that they are not there just to make a buck, that they are in business for the aid and comfort of the grain producers? The private grain trade has become fat from living off the backs of grain farmers for too many years in this country. Sometimes that requires aid and comfort from a national Government and the Parliament of Canada. To have legislation that niggles away at and undermines and seeks to destroy what our people have put together over 60 to 75 years is reprehensible and not acceptable.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. As Hon. Members will know, we are on Motion No. 30 which attempts to clarify a part of Clause 3 of the Western Grain Transportation Act, Bill C-155, which we have been discussing since yesterday. The pertinent motion deals with a part of Clause 3 which allocates four members to the

September 30, 1983
Western Grain Transportation Act
Senior Grain Transportation Committee. These members would be active grain growers holding Canadian Wheat Board permit books. The point which is at issue here, at this point in time, is a further provision in that clause which has created a space on the Senior Grain Transportation Committee for these four producers. It goes on to say that these four producers must not be from a category which they go on to spell out.
Clause 3(d) reads in part:
-at the time of their election, and for the duration of their service as members of the Committee-
These producers shall not be:
-nominees, officers, directors, agents or representatives of any corporation, board or cooperative, the business of which is the purchase, sale, storage, processing or transportation of grain-
The problem which has arisen since we dealt with this clause is that we have been receiving conflicting legal opinions as to whether that prohibition would apply to a farmer who is a member of his local Wheat Pool committee or his United Grain Growers local committee, or whether it would apply to and include people who have been delegates to the United Grain Growers annual meeting, or delegates to the various pool organizations in the three Provinces. There are conflicting opinions as to whether those delegates would or would not be eligible to serve on the Senior Grain Transportation Committee.
These delegates include a great number of farmers who are very interested in the transportation of grain and the good of their community. To make certain these people are not prohibited from seeking election to the Senior Grain Transportation Committee under that clause which allows one member from Alberta, one farmer from Manitoba and two farmers from Saskatchewan, we have proposed Motion No. 30, which says:
(0 nothing in paragraph (d) shall prevent elected local committee members and delegates of grain co-operatives and the officers of farming corporations and co-opcratives from being eligible for election to the Senior Grain Transportation Commitlcc.
This is to be inserted for greater clarity, Mr. Speaker, to make absolutely certain that at no time would there be a court ruling which would declare a farmer ineligible to be a member of the Senior Grain Transportation Committee simply because he was either a delegate to one of the three Prairie pools or to the annual meeting of the United Grain Growers. It would also clarify the position of farmers who are members of local seed cleaning co-operatives which are in the business of storage and processing of grain. It would make them eligible for the Senior Grain Transportation Committee without any argument as to the interpretation.
There is some doubt whether some members of co-operative farms, particularly if they have some seed cleaning as part of their operation, would be eligible now. The inclusion of this amendment would make it quite clear that the intention of the Bill is not to reduce the eligibility of farmers who are very active in their local communities and in the grain trade at the
local level. It would permit them to seek a post on the Senior Grain Transportation Committee.
We support this motion on the understanding that any elected position in a democracy should be as wide open as possible. There is a requirement that the people who seek this particular position must be active holders of a Canadian Wheat Board permit book, which means they are active farmers. That requirement rules out any full-time president of a grain company. It would make it very difficult for them to continue because most of them have been required, through the exigencies of their work with the grain co-operatives, to lease their land to someone else, which makes them no longer an active farmer. So I think the concern behind the Bill as it now stands may have been extended a little too far and instead has created a lot of doubt as to whether ordinary farmers who take part in their local community organizations, including the UGG and the pools, are eligible to seek election. It would broaden the base of those eligible to be part of the Senior Grain Transportation Committee.
I urge both sides of the House to reconsider the clause to broaden the base and allow for the widest democratic participation possible, and to support this motion as it now stands before us.

Mr. Speaker, the motion before us, Motion No. 30, submitted by the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin), is a very important one, one on which I hope we can use reason in the House rather than just having the Government or, indeed, the Conservative Party sitting idly by on it. The reason I feel this way is that there is a real possibility that thousands of prairie farmers could be prevented from seeking office on the Senior Grain Transportation Committee if Clause 3, which, by the way, was moved by the Conservative Party and supported by the Liberal Party-
How do you know? You weren't there.

-in the Committee this summer, carries. I would ask the Hon. Member for Portage-Marquette (Mr. Mayer) to stand and tell the House his interpretation of this particular clause. I think, very seriously, that if the heckling could be kept down, Hon. Members would find this to be a very important part of our debate.
Clause 3 states that four members who are active producers can be elected to the Senior Grain Transportation Committee. It states that there might be one for Manitoba, two for Saskatchewan and one for Alberta. We should follow the next portion very carefully, particularly those Hon. Members in the House who are also lawyers, and Your Honour is included. It states:
-who, at the time of their election, and for the duration of their service as members of the Committee, are not nominees, officers, directors, agents or representatives of any corporation, board or co-operative, the business of which is the purchase, sale, storage, processing or the transportation of grain-

Western Grain Transportation Act
I understand the reason this clause was inserted concerning many of the people who will be sitting on the Senior Grain Transportation Committee. It is a conflict of interest clause. That means that if a representative of one of the elevator companies or the railways or anyone else who is to be on the Senior Grain Transportation Committee is represented in that way, then that same person should not be seeking office as a producer. In many cases this type of clause is obviously needed.
However, the problem with the clause is that when the word "co-operative" is inserted, it is dealing with the structure of the Wheat Pools on the Prairies. I think many Hon. Members do not understand that the Wheat Pools on the Prairies involve a very grass roots issue, a decentralized kind of structure. Every country elevator in my Province and across the Prairies has a Wheat Pool committee. Approximately 800 of those committees exist in the Province of Saskatchewan alone. Between 10 and 20 farmers are members of each committee.
We have heard at least one legal opinion that says it is possible, and 1 think one could so construe in a court of law, that a representative of a company could be a Wheat Pool committee man. These Wheat Pool committee men do not have a great deal of power, but they do have some power over what happens in local country elevators. They also meet every year. At their annual meetings they pass resolutions requesting the head office or the Wheat Pool to take certain positions on issues of great importance to the farmers. As I said, this involves hundreds of different Wheat Pool committees and thousands, maybe even tens of thousands, of prairie farmers.
If lawyers were able to persuade the courts that a representative of any corporation, board or co-operative would mean the chairman, the secretary or an ordinary member of a Wheat Pool committee, then this clause in the Bill would disenfranchise thousands of prairie farmers.
In all seriousness, perhaps the Hon. Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski), who is the Conservative Party spokesman, or another Conservative might give us the legal interpretation as to what Clause 3 really means.
Why don't you hire a lawyer?

Why do I not hire a lawyer? The Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) is an excellent lawyer and 1 would invite him to look at Clause 3 and advise the House whether or not an officer could indeed be the secretary of a Wheat Pool committee, chairman of a Wheat Pool committee or an ordinary member of a Wheat Pool committee.
I will look at it next week.
He wants to charge us first before he gives us a legal opinion.
It will be a legal aid case for the NDP.
I invite Members of the Conservative Party to take a serious look at this.
Why don't you be serious?
I am being very serious. Incidentally, not a single Member from the Conservative Party has spoken to this motion.
It is a nothing motion, that is why.

Then why do you not get up and say that? I would like to see a Member of the Conservative Party get up and tell us why he believes that a Wheat Pool secretary, president or committee member would not be disenfranchised from seeking office to the Senior Grain Transportation Committee.
He is not excluded and you know it.

We have lawyers who say that it is not unreasonable to interpret that a representative of a co-operative could be a Wheat Pool committee man. If that is the case, we will then have a situation where thousands of people will be disenfranchised. This also refers directly to the word "agent". A Wheat Pool agent in a small town or village may not be able to seek office on the Senior Grain Transportation Committee as well. If that is the case, I think it is very unfair that so many ordinary, hard working farmers are being excluded from being elected to the office of a member of the Senior Grain Transportation Committee.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Axworthy) and Members on all sides of the House should take a very close look at this. The Wheat Pools are very decentralized. They practise a great degree of economic democracy in terms of having thousands of their members involved in running the local elevator and trying to run the Wheat Pool at a provincial and national level as well.
The same thing could perhaps apply to a co-op farm. There are a number of co-op farms in this country. Would someone who is a director of a co-op farm be excluded from seeking office because Clause 3 states that officers, directors and agents cannot seek office? Are directors of a co-op farm, which might indeed be an ordinary small farm, excluded from seeking office? What about a small family farm that has been incorporated? There are many such farms in my riding and I ask whether they would be excluded from seeking office. The Member for Vegreville is shaking his head; I can hear it from here. Please get up and tell us what you are saying. I can hear his head rattling but I cannot understand what he is saying.
This clause of the Bill could deny thousands of people on the Prairies the right to seek office. This also applies to the United Grain Growers, to a corporate farm, to a co-operative farm and, of course, to the Wheat Pools. I believe the Wheat Pools in this country are much too important to be left out of the scheme of things as far as this committee is concerned.

It is my understanding that a number of lawyers who have studied this issue have taken different positions. If there is any doubt, why do we not insert a clause in the Bill similar to that suggested by the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) which makes it abolutely clear that the target here is not the ordinary farmer who has a permit book but the senior officer of a company, an agent of a company or a senior representative of a company. If there is a legal opinion that is different from that which we heard from two lawyers at the committee which would exclude individual producers who happen to be directors of local pools, local UGGs, or members of a family farm that operates as a corporation or co-operative farm, we are not in favour of that either.
I hope I have put enough on record so that the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) will not have to get up again to ask what our position is.

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted that we are finally hearing a spokesperson from the Official Opposition speak on the amendment introduced by the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin).
We are concerned about the makeup of the Senior Grain Transportation Committee. We feel that it is a committee that can have an important role to play. There is still some debate about whether this will be a technical committee or an advisory committee. I wish to put on record the testimony given to the Transport Committee by Mr. Arthur Kroeger, Secretary, Ministry of State for Economic Development, as reported at page 125:44 of the proceedings of that committee as follows:
Mr. Chairman, I do not think the committee is intended as was suggested to this committee by Mr. Turner of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool. I do not think it is intended that this committee would be limited to narrow technical functions. It is true that to deal with some of the major issues in the grain transportation system at present, you have to look at some of the specifics; you have to look at some technical matters. But the committee is intended to have broad advisory responsibilities, in the first instance to the administrator.
I think that illustrates that this can be more than just a technical committee.
We are concerned that as many producers as possible be eligible to sit on that committee. Out of this concern we are moving this amendment that clear up the ambiguity that exists in the amendment to Clause 3(d) of the proposed legislation.
We are concerned about this and I do not think it does the cause of the Official Opposition any good to belittle that concern. In fact, I think it raises the question of whether they share our concerns. Their attempt to belittle our position on this makes me wonder whether there is a double agenda involved. When the Conservatives moved the amendment that constitutes much of Clause 3(d), their intent was so obvious and blatant that they had to amend the original amendment. It was then accepted by the Liberals and Conservatives voting together.
How would you know? You were not there.

In the original amendment the part that they deleted was "-or elected or appointed representives of any board or committee involved in an advisory or other capacity with respect to the grain trade."
September 30, 1983

That last wording in the original amendment to Clause 3(d) would have made it even more obvious that members of the Wheat Pool who sit on advisory committees would have been eliminated from being eligible to sit on the Senior Grain Transportation Committee. It was so obvious that they had to withdraw that last part of the paragraph. To dispute that there is some ambiguity in this subclause is nonsense; it is there. Different legal opinions have admitted that ambiguity. In the opinion of some lawyers a reasonable interpretation of the words in that subclause could prevent a nominee of a co-operative chosen to be a delegate at a subdistrict committee meeting of grain producers from being elected or continuing to serve as a member of the committee.
Furthermore, it is possible to construe Subclause (d) as preventing a member of a local Wheat Pool advisory committee who sits as a representative of a co-operative from being elected or from continuing to serve as a member of the Senior Grain Transportation Committee. The proposed wording of Clause 3(d) does not go so far as to deny a member of a co-operative from being elected or from continuing to serve as a member of the Senior Grain Transportation Committee. There is honest ambiguity and there is honest doubt here.
Why are Members of the Conservative Party so adamant in opposing a very reasonable and innocent subamendment? If they are so in favour of having Wheat Pool members and delegates participating in the election of members to the Senior Grain Transportation Committee, why are they opposing this amendment?

Western Grain Transportation Act
The history of the co-operative movement in agriculture in western Canada is vital. It has played a very crucial role. The co-operative movement is the result of years of experience of farmers in Canada which led them to the conclusion that only through co-operative action can they defend their self-interest, that only through coming together, marketing their products together, are they able to prevent the exploitation which private grain dealers have been involved in for years and years. At one time, Mr. Speaker, the co-operative movement was totally opposed by the vested interests in this country, the people who operated the Grain Exchange out of Winnipeg and the private grain monopolies. And those grain monopolies had their interests represented in both the Liberal and Conservative Parties. These traditional Parties opposed the co-operative movement because it meant that their power over farmers would evaporate, that the farmers themselves would take control of their own destinies.
All progressive victories in the past have necessitated an ongoing struggle to maintain those victories. We see that with medicare, with social legislation, with all progressive legislation. Every progressive move brings forth a reaction. The fight against the co-operative movement, Mr. Speaker, is not over. That fight continues. We in this Party are determined to fight to protect the victories of the past. We are determined to fight to protect the pools and the co-operative efforts of farmers themselves. We will fight against any measure to erode the position of the farmers.
I can understand, perhaps, some of my Conservative friends being somewhat confused because a co-operative, like the Pools, Mr. Speaker, represents the producers. In the end it is a producers' organization. So producers involved in that organization, even though they might have various positions, are still first and foremost producers. They are not members of some corporation. They have created the Wheat Pool, which has many of the trappings of a corporation, but it is more than that. It is the product of the producers themselves. Ordinary producers, who are involved in advisory positions and in operating the Wheat Pools should not be labelled in the same way as one would label a manager of a private grain company or a private elevator.
I notice the Chair is indicating that my time is up. With the consent of the House I would request one more minute to conclude my remarks.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. And I wish to thank the House for this opportunity to conclude my remarks.
The point I was trying to make, Mr. Speaker, is that members of the Wheat Pools, whether in Alberta, Saskatchewan or Manitoba, who hold delegate positions or advisory positions are not really just officers or agents of a company. They are still producers involved in a co-operative effort with other producers. Their position is quite different to that of an

Western Grain Transportation Act officer of a private company. That is why I am dismayed that the words "or co-operative" is in here. To me it indicates that there is not a recognition that a producer who is active in his pool organization is not the same as a businessman who is involved in a private grain company. The other point I wish to make in summation, Mr. Speaker-and perhaps it is my major point-is that if there is agreement in the House that there is reasonable ambiguity in the subclause as it now exists, then I invite the House to give unanimous consent to the amendment, Motion No. 30, which has been introduced by my colleague, the Hon. Mr. Speaker, I am happy to rise again today to speak on what I consider to be a historic Bill. I believe everyone who has spoken on the motion today realizes that in later years someone will look back at the record to see who spoke and what they said today. Although my remarks may not be the most historic on record, I would like to add them to the debate.
1 have always had a great interest in historic law. If one had the opportunity to visit some of the ancient civilizations such as Egypt or Persia, one would find that the law was carved in stone. It was set up in such a way by the lawmakers that it would remain. There was a finality to the law. Good law which is made today has a permanence to it. Unfortunately, bad law has a permanence to it as well. This Bill, which will set up a way of handling grain in western Canada, if it passes, is very important. It is a Bill which will set down in a permanent way something which is extremely important to western Canadians.
Some of my colleagues to my right have indicated that not all the Hon. Members of the New Democratic Party took part in the committee hearings. That is exactly correct. I did not take part in the hearings myself. Nevertheless, I still feel that Parliament is a place in which Members can relate to the work of the Members who took part in the committee hearings. I also feel it is very important, when we come to the House of Commons, that we relate from our point of view to the legislation which is being discussed. Each Hon. Member here brings a different point of view. It is true that because of my vocation in life I do not have a quota book, 1 do not own a farm, I do not farm every year. However, farming in my part of the world is extremely important. Even though I do not have a quota book, and even though I was not at the committee hearings-and we all have a right to speak on the Bill-I feel it is extremely important that when something is being set down in stone, something is being put into law, we must be very sure in making that law that we protect the little person, the person at the bottom. In moving Motion No. 30 my colleague is trying to spell out in a concrete way that the person at the bottom, the representative of someone who belongs to a local grain co-operative, will not be excluded, ever. The mood which seems to exist in the country today sometimes argues against the notion of co-operatives. It is a mood which says that it is better to look after oneself, after
one person, than to have a group looking after everyone. I can see that sometime down the road a person who belonged to a co-operative might be discarded simply because of the mood against co-ops. That is why 1 would like to see this amendment in the Bill. I hear that Hon. Members down there are willing to accept it. It must be clear in the future that the little person will always be protected.
Another point I would like to bring forward is that those who were not present at all the committee hearings have a special reason for reading the Bill now and bringing forward their viewpoint. They can see it from their perspective but they do not have all the history. I would like to see it clearly spelled out in this part of the Bill that a representative of one group cannot come in as a representative of another group and thereby take two places. The reason 1 say this is that in the grain growing and handling business we have a lot of people whom I would call joiners. In church, in school, in political Parties, in business you will have a certain number of people whom I call joiners. They are people who get into various organizations at the same time. We can look at the various representatives of the grain associations in western Canada and we will find that there are many people who belong to four or five different groups. As some of my colleagues pointed out, they belong to pools, the UGG and so on. They are joiners, and that is probably one of the reasons why they became active in politics. I would like it spelled out that if a person is appointed to the Senior Grain Transportation Committee under one heading, he cannot come in under another heading as well.
I would call upon my colleagues around here, Mr. Speaker, to be very cautious of the fact that we are putting something down which can be interpreted in a different way by our sons, grandsons and greatgrandsons, unless it is spelled out very clearly today. All the motion put forward by the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) intended to do was to spell this out very clearly as it relates to people who are in co-operative associations. I was happy to hear the Hon. Member for Portage-Marquette (Mr. Mayer) say that he-and I am sure he is representing his Party-would be willing to accept this if there is any doubt. I feel there is a doubt. Our legal opinion indicates there is a doubt, and so I hope Members on the Government side and on our side will agree that the motion should be included there and that the Bill will be like the old laws written in stone, that it will be clear and simple enough for all to understand, and the ordinary, little person will be the one who will be protected all the time.
I am going to bring my remarks to an end now, Mr. Speaker, but I hope that everyone in the House will take to heart these few thoughts I have brought to the matter and that the little person will be protected all the time through this motion.

Mr. Speaker, I certainly want to support my colleague, the Hon. Member for Portage-Marquette (Mr. Mayer). Quite frankly, we are dealing with a motion which is really redundant, but in order that

there be no doubt we certainly will accept the spirit and thrust of what the NDP is proposing. In the course of the committee hearings, the Hon. Member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) stated:
It is not the intention of the Members on this side to prevent Members of local pools or UGG organizations from being elected or being named to this Committee.
The Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) knows that very well. He was there. Nonetheless, he continues to prompt his colleagues to distort the facts and mischievously to mislead Members of this House. The fact is that most of what we have heard today is nothing but clap-trap. What we on this side of the House tried to achieve was simply to ensure that producers, enfettered by any other biases, full-time producers who were in the business of farming and had no other biases or interests, were to be included in this very useful Senior Grain Transportation Committee.
Once again we witness the hypocrisy of the New Democratic Party. During the course of the committee meetings at one point in time the Hon. Member for Regina West discarded the Senior Grain Transportation Committee as being meaningless or irrelevant. He said, and I quote from page 126:106:
I would prefer that this whole damn thing he deleted or else be put under the aegis of the Canadian Wheat Board.
Now we hear from Members over there that this committee is going to transform the whole policy making mechanism for the grain transportation industry, yet at the same time the Hon. Member said that as far as he was concerned the whole damn thing should be deleted. They cannot have it both ways.
Watch your language.

Well, I am only quoting the Hon. Member for Regina West who uses that word more than all other Members put together.
It seems that the NDP does not want producers sitting on this committee, Mr. Speaker. It wants producers to be aligned with either the UGG or the pools or Cargill or CN or CP. What we were trying to do was to ensure that, say, a director of CN or CP who was a farmer could not serve on this committee. There is a former Member of this House who is now a chairman of one of the railroads and he has a Wheat Board permit. If that restriction is not put in place he could conceivably sit as a farm representative. I guess the NDP really wanted that sort of thing, but we did not. We wanted to clarify and make absolutely sure that these were bona-fide, full-fledged producers who were in the business of producing grain.
I hope the press hears that.

Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, we thought it was very important that these producers had the opportunity to square off with representatives from the railroads. The Members of the NDP do not want the railroads sitting at the same table as the farmers on the Senior Grain Transportation Committee. How absurd! How ridiculous! The fact of the matter is that if there is going to be any cohesion or co-ordination, if there is any way that we can cut out the finger-point-
Western Grain Transportation Act ing, that can take place during the course of the Senior Grain Transportation Committee's sittings. I see the former Minister of Transport applauding in support. I think he knows, as I know, that the only way to get this very complex and complicated system working is to bring representatives of all components of this very diverse system together and seat them around a table, get them all pulling in the same direction, dedicating themselves to a common cause, the discharging of their responsibilities and obligations.
1 can think of no other way in which a lot of the difficulties and problems, either real or potential, can be overcome and reduced to a minimum than through the Senior Grain Transportation Committee. We certainly support the concept. It was never our intention to be overly restrictive as far as the producers were concerned. We believe that these various organizations involved in the system can have their representatives, but we also very firmly believe that producers are very important. We consider that to be the reason for the whole structure in the first place. If it were not for producers producing grain, we would not need a Senior Grain Transportation Committee or a Grain Transportation Agency Administrator. Therefore, it is only natural that producers should serve on the committee.
The same is true with regard to other parts of the Bill. I do not know whether it was an oversight or whether it was deliberate, but the word "producer" was conspicuous by its absence. Quite frankly, we as Members on this side tried to incorporate the word "producers" at every opportunity. We also incorporated that any decisions taken by the Senior Grain Transportation Committee or the Grain Transportation Administrator would be taken in the best interests of the producer, in other words, maximizing returns for the producer. That is what we set out to do and that is what we will continue to do as we debate the Bill.
I repeat that the New Democratic party has tried maliciously to exaggerate and to use a red herring. As my colleague, the Hon. Member for Portage-Marquette indicated, it is trying to get back into the good graces of the Wheat Pools. In so doing, it is trying to do irreparable damage to the producer body. No one went to bat for the producers, certainly the NDP did not. It voted against it. Of course, the Wheat Pools did not give their support, believing that they could best represent the producers. We saw fit, and the Government supported our amendment, to incorporate Wheat Pool membership, strengthening it. We certainly apologize to no one and we think the Bill will be better as a result.
I rise on a point of order, Mr. Speaker. I wonder if 1 could have the permission of the House to ask a question of the Hon. Member who just sat down?

My question is perhaps technical, but it is with regard to Clause 3 of the Bill. Member for Kootenay West (Mr. Kristiansen), who is to speak next, will read into the record a legal opinion which raises some doubt as to whether or not these ordinary producer-farmers may actually seek office if they happen to belong to a local Wheat Pool committee. Mr. Speaker, I think the Hon. Member for the question because my colleague, the Hon. Member for Portage-Marquette answered it. If the Hon. Member would want to familiarize himself with the evidence that was taken at the committee, I would refer him to the passage in Committee Proceedings No. 125, at pages 28 and 29. As reported in Issue No. 125, at pages 87 and 88, the Hon. While the Hon. Member for Regina West understood perfectly the intentions of the Members of the Conservative Party when they moved the amendment, he has obviously been influenced by other Members of his Party because he is now suggesting that there was a deliberate attempt to exclude the delegates, the locals of the Wheat Pools, and the UGG. Member for Portage-Marquette pointed out, to remove any question of doubt we are certainly prepared to accept the thrust and the principle of the NDP motion.
