Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) and the New Democratic Party, I am glad to accept the conversion of the Hon. Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski)-
Oh, oh!
-and supposedly that of his colleagues. I seem to recall his saying just a few moments ago that our amendment was both redundant and unnecessary.
It is.

In dealing with the subject, I would now like to read into the record, under the letterhead of the House of Commons, a letter to the Hon. Member for Regina West from Mr. R. Cosman, the Assistant Parliamentary Counsel to the House, dated September 29, 1983. It states:
In response to a request from Mr. Daryll Richards of your office, I have reviewed the amendment proposed with respect to paragraph (d) of Clause 3 of Bill C-155 as contained in the seventeenth report of the Standing Committee on Transport.
It is my opinion that a reasonable interpretation of the words of that paragraph could prevent a "nominee" of a co-operative chosen to be a delegate at a subdistrict committee meeting of grain producers from being elected or continuing to serve as a member of the Senior Grain Transportation Committee.
Furthermore, it is reasonably possible to construe paragraph (d) as preventing a member of a local wheat pool advisory committee who sits as a "representative" of a co-operative from being elected or continuing to serve as a member of the Senior Grain Transportation Committee, as well.
The proposed wording of paragraph 3(d), however, does not go so far as to deny a member of a co-operative from being elected or continuing to serve as a member of the Senior Grain Transportation Committee.
In forming my opinion, I have taken the position that if I were advocating the non-eligibility of a "nominee" of a co-operative or the removal from membership of a "representative" of a co-operative with respect to the Senior Grain Transportation Committee, could the words of paragraph 3(d) reasonably be interpreted to support my position, and I find that they do, notwithstanding that it may not have been the original intention of the drafters of this particular provision to have such an effect.
1 am gratified to know that we are on good grounds. We felt that we were from the beginning, even if my Party was not certain, even if the Conservative Party was not certain, and even if the Liberal Government was not certain.
Certainly the letter I just quoted gives more than enough grounds for reasonable doubt that we were right in our opinion that these people may have been excluded, albeit inadvertently. Surely it is incumbent upon the representatives of ordinary people, especially Members from the western grain producing Provinces, to resolve the question in such a way that the benefit of the doubt goes to the representatives of co-operatives and those other organizations. If that is not done, what right do Members from the prairie Provinces have to claim even that they try to represent the best interests of the people who sent them here?

Mr. Speaker, 1 rise on a point of order. I would like to put a question to the Hon. Member for Portage-Marquette (Mr. Mayer) and the Hon. Member for Vegreville, both of whom may choose to answer or have another Conservative answer on their behalf. our credentials challenged. 1 have been a British Columbian and a resident of the West Kootenays long enough to know that if you scratch an interior resident of British Columbia you will find a hayseed close beneath the surface. Speak for yourself.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Could the Hon. Member indicate, with that type of rhetoric, why he will be supporting our amendment if it is redundant?

If the Hon. Member would be kind enough to wait until I reach that point in my presentation, he will find out. The objective behind introducing motions such as the one before us was undoubtedly just to delay the matter and give an opportunity to the Hon. Member for Spadina to talk about rent controls in Toronto. I do not know what that has to do with the Bill before us.
The same corporation.

Perhaps it was so that the NDP Members could present themselves as the saviours of the co-op movement. I know and have the support of very many people in the co-op movement. I am aware that these are very reasonable and business-oriented people. They must be to be in that movement. For that reason, when it comes time to vote, I can assure you that they will vote 99 percent in favour of the Progressive Conservative Party rather than the NDP.
We have heard fears raised about what would happen if a farming family incorporated itself or if two or three families got together and formed a production co-operative. I will read the existing Clause 3(d), Mr. Speaker, from line 30. It reads:
-who, at the time of their election, and for the duration of their service as members of the committee are not nominees, officers, directors, agents or representatives of any corporation, board or co-operative, the business of which is the purchase, sale, storage, processing or transportation of grain;-
Members of the NDP would have us believe that because a farmer loads up his truck and drives it for eight miles to the elevator, he is in the business of the transportation of grain. They would have us believe that because he buys his seed grain, he is in the business of buying and selling grain. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that there is not a court in the land that would put that interpretation on the words contained in Clause 3(d).
I was very pleased with the way our position was presented in committee by the Hon. Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazan-kowski) and his many colleagues who put in so many hours of work on that committee. I was very pleased by the way they fought for the grain producers of Canada. I think they have achieved a considerable victory by having incorporated on the Senior Grain Transportation Committee four representatives of the primary producers of Canada.
Hear, hear!

It is essential, Sir, that the representatives of these primary producers be free from any possible conflict of interest. They should be able to concentrate only from the point of view of the producers. For that reason, not just any permit book holder may be permitted to be the producer representative because, as the Hon. Mr. Speaker, I am pleased that we have an amendment which covers the ground that all of us are anxious to cover, although 1 must say that the Minister is worrying unnecessarily. Motion No. 31
That Bill C-155 be amended in Clause 10 by adding immediately after line 20 at page 6 the following:
"(c) a person who in his opinion represents labour in the handling and transportation of grain".

Mr. Speaker, 1 am very pleased to be able to speak to this amendment. I have been a trade unionist for 28 years. I strongly hope that we can have agreement in the House that labour should be represented on this important national board. There may have been better ways of organizing grain transportation, but if there is going to be a board like this, it will have an important function. Therefore, it is quite important that there be labour representation on it, as this motion provides.
There will be a number of different major jurisdictions concerned. There are the grain cleaners, grain loaders, the various stages of handling, the elevator employees, the railway workers, the longshoremen, the seamen, that is if Canada ever goes back to having a merchant marine. All these people ought to have a voice on this Grain Transportation Committee.
The basic principle is occasionally recognized in our country, but is not recognized often enough. The principle is simply that the people who do this work could have a voice in the decisions. Whether it is in grain handling at the beginning, the transportation, the loading, the grain handling at the other end, these are the people who do the work that create the surplus out of which wages are paid and profits are found. It is to the benefit of the country as a whole that they should have a voice in directing the work that they are doing. They are on the spot, they see what is needed and what is necessary for their health and safety.
I have 18 years' experience working in a factory which made corrugated paper boxes. I worked as a labourer in all departments, but mainly in the press department. I was a member of what is now the Canadian Paperworkers' Union. I could see day by day the value to the workers, but ultimately to a much wider circle, of having workers listened to in management decisions.
This was just one of 50 plants in this large North American corporation. There was no system of labour representation on any board of directors. Instead, we had to make do with negotiations and consultations between the union in our plant or the unions in other plants and the general management that represented only the large shareholders. Nevertheless, when we got a manager who was prepared to listen to the union, it turned out that not only working conditions and health and safety conditions in the plant were improved, but the plant became more efficient and productive for the benefit of both the workers and the company.
In this situation, the same applies, but there is a further consideration. In this situation the principal shareholder is the people of Canada. Considering the amount of money that has been put into the transportation system and the grain handling system in all of its forms, the pricipal investor in that whole system or complex is the people of Canada. There is, therefore, a more special reason why this principle should be embodied in the structure of the committee, namely, there should be some representation of labour, the people who actually do the work. This is quite distinct from putting in the representation, already provided for, of some of the major corporations that employ the labour. When only they are represented it turns out that they do not do a very good job in the long run because they do not understand the necessity of considering the health, welfare and wisdom of those who actually do the work.
Where public money is involved it is very important that the people doing the cleaning and loading of grain, the grain handling, whether at the elevators or ports, the longshoring and, when Canada comes to its senses and has a merchant marine, the people handling the boats offshore and in the lakes-all these people should have at least one voice in the management of the grain handling industry. They constitute the brain and muscle of a national network without which the grain cannot move to the ports, let alone beyond the ports. They should not be treated as mere muscle; they are brain and
September 30, 1983

muscle and spirit as well. Without their participation we will not have orderly and productive movement of grain.
I therefore urge all Parties in the House to support the amendment to have the Minister appoint a person who represents labour in the handling and transportation of grain.

Mr. Speaker, as we said in committee and on other occasions, we feel it is very important that all segments of the grain industry be represented, at least in an observer capacity. Some concern has been expressed by members of the grain producing community to the effect that they would like to find a way of bringing an action or communicating directly with the labour unions when they withdraw services and cause producers to lose money.
The amendment before us is much the same as that proposed by the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) in committee, although his was broader in scope. We supported that amendment.
When we look at the history of the grain handling sector of the economy, it is easy to see why it is important to have representation of some segment of the labour organizations involved in the movement of grain.
A strike began on May 16, 1982, which was settled on July 7, 1972, after 53 days. Ports in British Columbia were closed for 21 days in 1972. On July 26, 1973, a strike began which lasted 33 days. In 1974, grain handlers stopped work on October 10 and the strike lasted 44 days. At that time Mr. Vogel, the Chief Commissioner of the Canadian Wheat Board, said the strike was costing prairie farmers in western Canada $200 million in lost sales. In 1975, there was a 36-day walkout of grain weighers, a 24-day walkout by longshoremen and a one-day walkout by longshore-foremen. Dock workers at Montreal, Quebec City and Trois Rivieres went on strike for 25 days. In 1978, the strike on Canada's inland shipping fleet lasted for nine days. In 1981, a work stoppage at Thunder Bay lasted for 16 days. In November, 1982, there was another work stoppage.
By accepting the amendment we hope that the Parties involved in the movement of grain, including the unions- those in the grain terminals, the longshoremen and the railroading unions and all others-can be brought together with the four or five real grain producers in the Senior Grain Transportation Committee along with the management of those companies. This is why we think it would be effective for the grain producers to be unfettered and able to represent their fellow producers in discussions between the management of the terminal operators in Vancouver, the management of the railway companies, and the management of the line elevator companies, the people who are so important in the movement of grain.
We feel confident that if there is face to face discussion on the Senior Grain Transportation Committee among members of all segments of the industry, the movement of grain will go much more smoothly and no one will suffer. We therefore support the amendment.
Western Grain Transportation Act Mr. Jesse P. Flis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport): Mr. Speaker, I was a little disappointed that the Member of the New Democratic Party who spoke in support of the amendment did not explain to the House who this representative would be. Would he belong to the port union, the railway union, the elevator union? There are a lot of workers involved in grain handling who do not belong to any union but they are labour and should be represented. 1 listened intently, hoping to get some guidance on who the labour representative should be.
I agree that the representative of labour should be included as an observer. Of course, the choice is being left to the Minister, and that is as it should be. In the Transport Committee we inserted Clause 10(3) as follows:
The Minister may appoint, and
(a)	a person as his representative
That was so that there will be an observer present representing the Minister, but one who is not allowed to vote or take part in discussions. We also provided for:
(b)	a person who in his opinion represents the producers of crops in the Western Division for the shipment of which a Canadian Wheat Board permit is not required.
Such person could also act as an observer on the Senior Grain Transportation Committee.
I see nothing wrong with adding a representative of labour as well. This would not make the committee too large, which was a consideration of the Transport Committee. It would allow labour to monitor the meetings and have some indirect input. Some may argue that an observer does not have much say in the proceedings. When the Transport Committee was travelling across Canada and was considering the Bill clause by clause, many observers attended its meetings. As the Hon. Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) knows very well, some were from the railways, some from labour and some from the various producers. They talked to the committee members. They talked to us before the hearings and after the hearings. Members from all three Parties lobbied us. They played a very important role in the whole process. I see labour also playing a very important role by being given this observer status on the Senior Grain Transportation Committee.
I would also like to demonstrate to the New Democratic Party that if that Party brings in positive, constructive amendments to this Bill, we will support them. However, if that Party brings in frivolous amendments just to stall the debate and take the time of the House, then we will not support those amendments. The Government is prepared to support positive amendments such as this one. I am announcing to Hon. Members of the New Democratic Party that we, on this side of the House, are ready to support their amendment.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to see this type of amendment made to this Bill. I am a person who has had the good fortune to work within the labour ranks and from there to go into the role of management. In the

September 30, 1983
Western Grain Transportation Act Port of Vancouver I have had occasion to have many meetings, not only with the senior managers around the port activities but I have also had the pleasure of having hours of discussion with senior labour people. 1 can also remember some years back, when I was a new Member of this House, a group of us quietly going out to see what could be done to break one of the impasses between the longshormen's union, the Grain Workers Union and the railroad union. I made the observation that too often much of the trouble which develops in these confrontations is really created by people whose function it is to work at public relations or in the legal field, legal people and labour lawyers. It was our experience at that time that the impasse was broken only by getting the leaders on the labour side together with the senior people on the industrial side and bypassing the bureaucracy. That brought about a resolution to that particular impasse.
1 believe it is important that some of us who are management oriented realize that there is often more talent in managerial functions on the labour side than there is in the hierarchy of management.
In the Port of Vancouver we have had bottlenecks and unloading problems over the years. I had a conversation with Mr. Henry Kanes, the leader of the Grain Workers' Union, who gets absolutely frustrated with the inability of the industry to bring its parts together and to improve some of the inefficiencies. He feels that some of the inefficiencies caused by management is felt on the backs of the working men. 1 know the frustration which grain workers feel when they know there are simple arrangements which can increase the productivity of the port and the handling of the grain, and which would also increase the take-home pay packet of the grain worker. 1 speak, for instance, Mr. Speaker, of the simple act of the dispatching of grain cars for the elevators in the Port of Vancouver from Kamloops or to some other inland point where the assembly of the trains matches the delivery need of the elevators. I speak simply of enlarging the four-mile switching limit at the Port of Vancouver to 12 miles. These are suggestions which have come from labour. However, when you enlarge the switching limit from 4 miles to 12 miles you immediately run into the interests of the British Columbia railroad which probably has revenues which are dependent on the 4-mile switching limit. However, over-all, the Port of Vancouver could work to advantage on a 12-mile limit.
1 hope that if we put a labour observer into a committee that is as important as this one we can start to break down some of the artificial impediments to the improvements of the productivity of the whole movement system, because if we do not, the farmer is going to suffer along with the individual worker in the system. I feel it would do the attitude to this whole concept much good to bring labour more and more into this type of decision so that it can understand more and more of the problems of the farmer and of the manager. If we do not do this, we are going to have more and more people laid off and more and more labour strikes. We must work at explaining why decisions are made, and spread the knowledge and the reasons behind certain things which are being done. If we
could allow input from the working man into these decisions, I feel we would do much to improve the productivity which this country needs if it is to start creating more jobs and addressing our serious unemployment problem.
1 am very pleased to see all Parties in the House come together on the suggestion that labour should be involved. I feel this will go a long way toward creating a good working relationship for the future.

Mr. Speaker, we tried initially, if I recall, to have this done by way of the Minister appointing a voting member of the Senior Grain Transportation Committee from the trade union movement involved in the storage, handling, elevating, loading and unloading and transportation of grain. I do not recall whether I was ruled out of order or whether I was voted down. However, we would still prefer that. One of the major players in the whole system is the worker. However, if this is all we can get for now by way of agreement from the Government and from the Official Opposition, that is fine. It is a beginning. We in this Party are under no illusion that this is a giant step forward, but it is finally a recognition. In legislation which is already in place there is little or no attention paid to workers, nor is any opportunity provided for workers to have some input. The railway workers are represented by somewhere between 15 and 20 different unions. With the grain handlers, one major union and a smaller one are involved. There are two or three unions representing the Great Lakes seamen, the deck officers and the engineers. The Grain Services Union represents country elevator employees in Saskatchewan and Manitoba, and some head office employees. There are the terminal elevator employees. There is the Electrical Workers Union. This adds up to about 30 or 35 unions which represent probably in the order of 100,000 workers.
It was interesting to see, Mr. Speaker, the input of individual trade union members and organizations prior to the hearings of the Transport Committee at the time we were holding the hearings, and following. I believe two different federations of labour and at least one city labour council presented briefs to the committee. The Grain Services Union representative appeared on behalf of many hundreds of country elevator agents. Surely that is a good indication, Mr. Speaker, in fact convincing evidence that the workers want to be included. They are in fact interested, they want to do a good job, and they want the opportunity. They have something to contribute. They know about the day-to-day operations in much greater detail and depth than a lot of their managers and foremen do.
The Parliamentary Secretary was wondering how the Minister would go about appointing that person. Well, it seems to me you will have to consult with the Canadian Labour Congress, the umbrella organization, which in turn would need to consult with all its member unions and probably strike a committee to get together and select from their number a person whom the Minister could appoint as an observer. It would not necessarily be the same person every year. Maybe
September 30, 1983

you could have two different people each year, one year someone from the grain handlers union, another year someone from the railway brotherhood, or some other organization. 1 would think the CLC would be the most convenient vehicle, or else the Minister himself could consult with the trade union organizations and the CLC and strike a committee of all unions involved in all aspects of grain handling and transportation. He could have them select from one of their number a person he can appoint as an observer.
I am assuming that this person who was there as an observer would at least have a voice but no vote. If all he can do is to sit there and observe, then you might as well mail him a copy of the minutes and he can stay home. But when there is a problem among the unions, or something like that, the union observer will be consulted and asked to participate in the meetings of the Senior Grain Transportation Committee to offer solutions, ideas, suggestions and tell the committee what their problems are. But if he is not going to have a voice, then he can stay home, read the minutes and save the expense of going to the meetings.
Let me illustrate an area we heard about in committee, especially from the railroads and once in a while from a Government Member and some other organizations, this business of weekend loading of railway cars at country elevators. 1 can tell you that the grain service union representing country elevator agents, and the elevator companies, when they co-operated with the railroads to spot some cars Friday night, they loaded them Saturday and Sunday for pick up Sunday night or Monday morning, there were a number of instances where this was done. The railroads brought the cars in, the employees and the elevator company worked like dogs over the weekend, loaded the cars, and a week later they were still sitting there. But they are willing to co-operate.
There is some dispute between the elevator agents and some of the grain companies regarding the 40 hours a week. I believe they can work it out because it is very similar to the dispute at the time when the 40 hour week was adopted in 1950 in the railroads. They can work it out and I am sure they will. But on the whole matter of weekend loading, both the elevator companies and the elevator agents as well as the grain services' unions can be most helpful. It is just a case of not listening to the railroads only, as has been to damn the case over the years.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that I can get confirmation from the Parliamentary Secretary that not only will the observer have a voice but also that it will be the intention of the Government at some early date to provide for a voting member, at least one, from the trade union movement involved in the transportation of grain. When I was on the railroad myself, heavily involved in the strike of 1950, which all of us hated, over the 40 hours a week, and in every episode since, much of the difficulty and problems which led or contributed to a breakdown and a strike or lock-out could have been avoided if there had been a lot more involvement from the unions in the day-to-day operations and year-to-year decision making, whether it is on technological change or on how to do something more efficiently. The
Western Grain Transportation Act
Hon. Member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) is perfectly correct; it is not only the grain handlers union in Vancouver. If you talk to railroaders in Vancouver, Winnipeg and Thunder Bay, the mess which passes for a distribution system in those three locations is incredible. In the name of competition you have two or three railroads running all over the darn city using up valuable land which could be used for houses, when they could all be running on the same set of three or four tracks instead of having a dozen tracks all over the city. The railway brotherhood unions have a contribution to make in this area.
If the Government were willing to reconsider and bring in an amendment of its own, I am certain we could have unanimous consent to increase the voting members of this committee by one or two. So what? Bring in an amendment, in which case I would be glad to withdraw my own. Add one or two more representatives selected by the trade union movement and appointed by the Minister. That would go a long way toward helping in this massive task which all the players have. It would help to head off in advance potential misunderstandings, breakdowns in communication, and confrontation. It would help to head off a lot of that. My own experience as both an employee and an employer is that when you had people working with you and not for you, you got a lot more work done, and done a lot better, and you had a much more loyal group of employees no matter what the size of the operation. But the present practices of management have brought about troubles of their own making, so I hope the Parliamentary Secretary, in response to my question, will be permitted to confirm that the observer will have a voice. I know he cannot have a vote. The Government should consider, during the course of report stage, bringing an amendment of its own to add one or two more people to the committee who would be appointed with a voice from the trade union movement.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to enter the discussion very briefly at this point on, I am happy to say, a more peaceful tone perhaps than some of the previous incursions. First of all, I should like to give support to the amendment submitted in the name of the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin), particularly as I am one who has had considerable direct experience in the involvement of employees in management decision-making, in fact in the company in which I am still on the seniority list. That was an experiment which produced healthy results in my own community. At least they were good results until the "BCRICing" of that company in British Columbia, an Act which terminated any local management, not to mention employee involvement in that management.
It was a worth-while experience, and 1 think it was generally recognized as such by Parties all around that table and in that given community. Because of that experience and my own

September 30, 1983
Western Grain Transportation Act
belief in the worth of such exercises, even if it is just representation in an observer capacity, as is mentioned in the amendment, I would particularly like to say how pleased I was to hear the comments of the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) a few minutes ago, a Member with whom I often find myself in disagreement, even if we do not argue directly very often. My experience is much the same as his, that when representatives of working people and representatives of the management side of industry are able to work together over extended periods of time wearing a common hat, there is a greater understanding and non-conflict created during the long process of non-conflict situations which can be very useful in overcoming some of these instances which must of necessity occur from time to time in the adversary relationship that takes place around collective bargaining. There is a great deal to be said for the kind of common understanding that is built during such a period. That is an essential lesson in conflict management, one which this nation and its component parts really must learn if we are to continue to survive and grow as a nation and as a community in the way we should.
I would also like to say that I appreciate what seems to be the tone adopted so far by Members from all corners of the House in the debate on this particular amendment. In so doing, 1 would also like to pay tribute, which I think is appropriate, to one of my colleagues who succeeded, together with the stroke of rationality that struck both the Government and the Official Opposition, in having the thrust of his last amendment accepted. As one who studies more than just human behaviour from time to time, I would like to quote briefly from a text which 1 believe to be appropriate, particularly to the Hon. Member for Regina West but also to the process in which we are engaged. In a book entitled "On Aggression" by Konrad Lorenz, some time is spent discussing the habits of a species of bird called jackdaws, which is actually the second most common variety of crow, a species which seems rather appropriate to our discussion. It states:
In jackdaws, and in many other very social birds, ranking order leads directly to protection of the weaker ones.
It continues:
Since high-ranking jackdaws, particularly males, interfere in every quarrel between two inferiors, this graduation of social tension has the desirable effect that the higher-ranking birds always intervene in favour of the losing party.
In jackdaws, another form of "authority" is already linked with the ranking position which the individual has acquired by its aggressive drive. The expression movements of a high-ranking jackdaw, particularly of an old male, are given much more attention by the colony members than those of a lower-ranking, young bird. For example, if a young bird shows fright at some meaningless stimulus, the others, especially the older ones, pay almost no attention to his expressions of fear. But if the same sort of alarm proceeds from one of the old males, all the jackdaws within sight and earshot immediately take flight. Since, in jackdaws, recognition of predatory enemies is not innate but is learned by every individual from the behaviour of experienced old birds, it is probably of considerable importance that great store is set by the "opinion" of old, high-ranking, and experienced birds.
I believe many people in the farming communities of western Canada would join with me in giving credit to the Hon. Member for Regina West who is certainly, in my own caucus,
one of the oldest, highest-ranking and most experienced of old birds.
Some bird.

Mr. Speaker, just briefly I want to rise and associate myself with the expression of support that emanated from the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) and the Hon. Member for Kindersley-Lloydminster (Mr. McKnight). We certainly have no difficulty in supporting Motion No. 31, which provides for a person representing labour and the handling of the transportation of grain to attend all or any meetings of the Senior Grain Transportation Committee as an observer, and that appointment would obviously be made by the Minister. As has been said by myself and other Hon. Members, the importance of the Senior Grain Transportation Committee and the work that it will do centres around the hope that all components of the system will be represented at the table. It is fair to say that there are some perhaps who may well have wished that the unions, the labour movement, had been included as a system participant, because they are vitally and integrally involved in the transportation of grain.
As outlined in the interpretation section of the Bill, "system participant" means any corporation, partnership or organization engaged in the transportation of grain by rail or the shipping or handling of grain for transportation by rail as designated by the Governor in Council individually or by class. Because of the unique role that the labour movement plays in the orderly flow or movement of grain, I think a good argument could be made, because with that designation go some responsibilities as well.
I want to speak on the matter of reliability as an objective in our grain transportation system. Throughout the Bill, the original draft of the Bill, one sees the objective of the grain handling and transportation as being efficient and effective. We in our Party tried to incorporate the word "reliability" at every occasion possible. We felt that that was a clear objective and, that the Senior Grain Transportation Committee should cite it as an objective, because I think that if there is anything that has tarnished and damaged our reputation as a supplier of grain, it would probably not exceed the concept of reliability. In order for Canada to reap the kind of sales that it needs in the competitive marketplace and to receive the kind of premium prices that we hope to achieve, reliability becomes paramount.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Kindersley-Lloydmin-ster outlined a number of labour disruptions that have occurred over the last ten year and which have certainly hurt Canada's reputation as a reliable supplier of grain, and that goes without saying. To the extent that we can reduce the kind of labour disruption that occurs which, in turn, would reduce the disruption of the smooth and orderly flow of grain to all ports and hence to our markets, anything we could do in the
September 30, 1983

Bill to achieve that goal would certainly be a step in the right direction.
I certainly welcome the motion that has been advanced. As the Hon. Member for Kindersley-Lloydminster indicated, we did support the concept in committee and we will certainly support it now. I simply want to repeat that we have a grain transportation and handling system that is very complex. It depends upon the decisions of a great many people. It depends upon whether we face the challenges of geography. Naturally, we will be faced with strikes and labour disruptions, but we hope we can reduce those to a minimum and thereby increase the potential earnings of the producer. I think that the word "reliability", as a logical goal in achieving a worthwhile grain transportation and handling system, is something for which we should all strive. It ties in very closely with our other thrust, namely the need to maximize returns to the producers. That should be the bottom line objective of our efforts with this Bill in order to ensure that they receive top dollars for their grain and that they can move their grain rather than store it and have it become a very costly item in terms of storage and lost revenue.
Let me repeat the importance of having everyone at the table. Again I must say that it boggles my mind when the NDP suggests that representatives of the railways should not sit or the Senior Grain Transportation Committee. It is incomprehensible and certainly illogical.
1 think there is sufficient latitude under Clause 10 for the Minister to appoint a person as his representative or a person who, in his opinion represents the producers of crops in the western division for the shipment of which a Canadian Wheat Board permit is not required. 1 think, to that extent, that we can allow the Senior Grain Transportation Commitee to have observers. If we include a union representitive, that will certainly be of assistance in having all components at the bargaining table. I also find it strange that the NDP, which dismissed the Senior Grain Transportation Committee as a non-entity, is now suggesting that it is a pretty important component of this legislation. I presume that by the process of osmosis they are either getting hooked or led into supporting this Bill, it seems they have come a long way from their original stance when debate on this Bill began. At that time they said they would do everything in their power to obstruct it and everything possible to ensure that the Bill did not move forward an inch in the House of Commons. We now see them proposing constructive amendments, as the Parliamentary Secretary alluded to earlier.
If there is any confusion in anyone's mind, it certainly must be in the minds of the supporters of the NDP because they are now making a strong case for having all components of the system, except the railways, represented on the Senior Grain Transportation Committee. I believe that they sense that this committee will have a great amount of influence over future policies of grain handling and transportation in Canada.
Western Grain Transportation Act
1 think it goes without saying that while it is important to have a representative on the Senior Grain Transportation Committee, it is also important that he carries with it an obligation. When the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) makes his pitch to have labour represented, I hope he recognizes that the farmers of Canada will be looking to that labour representative for some leadership in ensuring that the rank and file workers, who can either allow the shipments to proceed or to stop, act responsibly. 1 hope it is taken for granted that the producers and all other representatives on the Senior Grain Transportation Committee will be expecting the labour movement to discharge its responsibility in a manner which will not impair the orderly movement of grain and that the labour representative will ensure that that happens.

Mr. Speaker, I also rise to speak in support of this motion, particularly as it relates to the labour unions and workers being represented on the Grain Transportation Committee. One of the problems which farmers face is strikes. When there is even a rumour of a strike in the Prairies there is a great deal of concern on the part of the farmer. Usually those strikes come at a time when there is a maximum need for the movement of grain which is at the end of July or following road ban time or when there has been a glut of grain. As the Hon. Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) noted, at that time the bins are bulging and storage is needed.
It is most important that there be a representative of labour on this committee so that dialogue can take place between all of the players. I think it is important to point out that this is the direction our Party has taken through the debate.
1 wrote down three words expressed by the Hon. Member for Vegreville which I believe exemplify the direction in which the committee has attempted to head. There are "fair and equitable representation of all segments".
Let me deal with the question of fairness. Certainly it would only be fair to have some representation from the labour to present its views as it is fair to have producers, grain companies, rail companies, commissioners and the Wheat Board. On the other hand, it is interesting to note that the NDP has decided that it does not want representatives from the railroads, if one can believe that. How can problems be negotiated in the Senior Grain Transportation Committee if all of the players are not represented around the table?
The Hon. Member then referred to equality. Since I had the privilege of being the first to speak-other than a couple of words from the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin)-I can go back to the basics that were laid out in Motion No. 27 which amended exactly the same thing that was introduced in Motion No. 26. We simply have a continuation of that in dealing with the members who relate very directly to the Grain Transportation Committee.
I am very happy to see the progress that is being achieved in the House. It is the direction that our Party believed we could achieve from the outset in the committee and at report stage as well. In our motion, we wanted equality for the grain compa-

Western Grain Transportation Act nies; three representatives from each grain company, three from the line companies and three from the co-operatives. 1 believe that is fair and equitable. We have now reached that goal. We wanted representation from the primary producer, and the amendment put forward by my colleague for Kinders-iy-Lloydminster (Mr. McKnight) achieved that in committee with one producer from Alberta, two from Saskatchewan and one from Manitoba-none of which was directly related to the grain companies.
It is most important that we have someone from labour represented on the greater Grain Transportation Committee which can represent its problems about the bottlenecks that exist and also relate to the problems that farmers have in moving their grain.

Mr. Speaker, I realize that five o'clock is coming close. I believe, however, that we have had a pretty good examination of this particular amendment. As my Parliamentary Secretary has indicated, again we share the sentiments of the other side of the House and we believe that this is a useful amendment and we are prepared to adop it. I would hope that we could call the question on this issue so that on Monday we could start fresh on a brand new set of ideas and issues.
Before doing that, however, I would like the agreement of the House to spend a short minute or two on something that I would like to express to the House.
Agreed.

I would simply say that I agree with the spirit of the amendment but I want to qualify it to this extent:
1 think it is very important that, as the Minister making such an appointment, I have a way of doing so that would be acceptable to the union movement as well as make it easier for me to expedite my duties. I would want to offer a suggestion. 1 believe there is a transportation grain handlers' subcommittee of the CLC. I would suggest that I work with them or have them put forward nominations of that kind so that they would be able to choose a person who would best reflect the various union interests. I know there are several major unions of that kind involved and I would prefer to have them make the nomination, which I could in turn respond to. Perhaps 1 could be in contact with the President of the CLC to work out some arrangement of that kind to make sure there was a broad base of support.
With that qualification, Mr. Speaker, I wonder if we could have the agreement of the House to call the question on this particular amendment.
